text: Terraform's CLI is a single, self-contained binary with no runtime to install alongside it, and no dependency chain to untangle first. Once it's on your machine, how does it actually know how to talk to Azure or AWS? That's the provider model, and it's the first thing to understand before you write a single line of HCL — it explains why this course keeps saying 'Terraform plus a provider' instead of just 'Terraform.'

On Windows, winget install HashiCorp.Terraform or choco install terraform downloads terraform.exe and puts it on your PATH, same as you'd expect from any package manager. Prefer installing by hand instead? HashiCorp publishes a matching zip for your OS and architecture at releases.hashicorp.com — unzip it onto your PATH and you're done. Either way, confirm it worked with terraform version, which should print something like Terraform v1.9.x. There's nothing else to configure; it's genuinely just a binary.

Here's the part that surprises people coming from Bicep: the terraform binary itself has no idea what Azure is, or AWS either. Core Terraform only does a small set of generic things — parse your HCL configuration files, build a dependency graph of the resources you've declared, diff your desired config against a state file, and produce a plan of creates, updates, and deletes to get from one to the other. None of that logic is cloud-specific, and that's deliberate: it's what lets one CLI manage Azure, AWS, Google Cloud, Kubernetes, and hundreds of other systems with the same workflow.

So where does the cloud-specific logic actually live? In a provider — a plugin, built and versioned separately from Terraform core, whose entire job is translating Terraform's generic instructions into real API calls against one specific system. hashicorp/azurerm knows how to talk to the Azure Resource Manager API. You declare it in a required_providers block: source names the publisher and provider on the Terraform Registry, version constrains which releases are acceptable so an unexpected major upgrade can't silently change behavior, and the separate provider block holds configuration like features, which azurerm requires even when left empty.

That's the whole model: one cloud-agnostic engine on top, swappable provider plugins underneath, each one downloaded and versioned on its own. Next lesson, you'll put that provider to work for real — terraform init downloads it into your working directory, and you'll walk through plan and apply in depth, including what those plus, minus, and tilde symbols in the output actually tell you before anything real ever changes.
